claim: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) contains projection neurons that release the neurotransmitters dopamine, GABA, and/or glutamate from distal synapses.
source: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) contains projection neurons that release the neurotransmitters dopamine, GABA, and/or glutamate from distal synapses.
evidence: This is a foundational statement about VTA neuron types supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: VTA contains GABA neurons that synapse locally on to dopamine neurons.
source: VTA also contains GABA neurons that synapse locally on to dopamine neurons, synapses widely credited to a population of so-called VTA interneurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and is a premise being examined in the study.

claim: Interneurons in cortex, striatum, and elsewhere have well-defined morphological features, physiological properties, and molecular markers.
source: Interneurons in cortex, striatum, and elsewhere have well-defined morphological features, physiological properties, and molecular markers, but such features have not been clearly described in VTA.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge about interneurons in other brain regions.

claim: Such features have not been clearly described in VTA.
source: Interneurons in cortex, striatum, and elsewhere have well-defined morphological features, physiological properties, and molecular markers, but such features have not been clearly described in VTA.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the lack of prior evidence.

claim: There is scant evidence that local and distal synapses originate from separate populations of VTA GABA neurons.
source: Indeed, there is scant evidence that local and distal synapses originate from separate populations of VTA GABA neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of existing literature and sets up the study's hypothesis.

claim: VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of parvalbumin project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Challenging previous assumptions, we found that VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of parvalbumin, somatostatin, neurotensin, or Mu-opioid receptor project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of somatostatin project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Challenging previous assumptions, we found that VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of parvalbumin, somatostatin, neurotensin, or Mu-opioid receptor project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of neurotensin project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Challenging previous assumptions, we found that VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of parvalbumin, somatostatin, neurotensin, or Mu-opioid receptor project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of Mu-opioid receptor project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
source: Challenging previous assumptions, we found that VTA neurons genetically defined by expression of parvalbumin, somatostatin, neurotensin, or Mu-opioid receptor project to known VTA targets including nucleus accumbens, ventral pallidum, lateral habenula, and prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical tracing data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: VTA GABA projection neurons make functional inhibitory synapses locally within VTA.
source: Moreover, we provide evidence that VTA GABA and glutamate projection neurons make functional inhibitory or excitatory synapses locally within VTA.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: VTA glutamate projection neurons make functional excitatory synapses locally within VTA.
source: Moreover, we provide evidence that VTA GABA and glutamate projection neurons make functional inhibitory or excitatory synapses locally within VTA.
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological recordings shown in Figures 5-7.

claim: Local collaterals of VTA projection neurons could mediate functions prior attributed to VTA interneurons.
source: These findings suggest that local collaterals of VTA projection neurons could mediate functions prior attributed to VTA interneurons.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data presented in the study.

claim: A common attribute of addictive drugs is their ability to increase dopamine release from VTA projections.
source: The ventral tegmental area (VTA) is a central component of the brain's reward circuitry, and a common attribute of addictive drugs is their ability to increase dopamine release from VTA projections (Lüscher, 2016; Nestler, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The VTA projects to nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral pallidum (VP), lateral habenula (LHb), and prefrontal cortex (PFC).
source: The VTA projects to and receives inputs from many brain structures involved in reward-related behavior, including nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral pallidum (VP), lateral habenula (LHb), and prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Fields et al., 2007; Morales and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The VTA receives inputs from nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral pallidum (VP), lateral habenula (LHb), and prefrontal cortex (PFC).
source: The VTA projects to and receives inputs from many brain structures involved in reward-related behavior, including nucleus accumbens (NAc), ventral pallidum (VP), lateral habenula (LHb), and prefrontal cortex (PFC) (Fields et al., 2007; Morales and Margolis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VTA neurons are highly heterogeneous.
source: However, VTA neurons are highly heterogeneous.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: The VTA contains distinct populations of DA neurons that can be segregated by gene expression, projection target, and function.
source: The VTA contains distinct populations of DA neurons that can be segregated by gene expression, projection target, and function (Azcorra et al., 2023; Poulin et al., 2020; Roeper, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GABA-releasing VTA neurons make local intra-VTA synapses.
source: GABA-releasing VTA neurons make local intra-VTA synapses (Bayer and Pickel, 1991; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2009), but also project widely outside the VTA, including dense projections to LHb, VP, and VP-adjacent areas of basal forebrain (Kaufling et al., 2010; Oades and Halliday, 1987; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: GABA-releasing VTA neurons project widely outside the VTA, including dense projections to LHb, VP, and VP-adjacent areas of basal forebrain.
source: GABA-releasing VTA neurons make local intra-VTA synapses (Bayer and Pickel, 1991; Omelchenko and Sesack, 2009), but also project widely outside the VTA, including dense projections to LHb, VP, and VP-adjacent areas of basal forebrain (Kaufling et al., 2010; Oades and Halliday, 1987; Taylor et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 25% of VTA glutamate neurons co-express a DA marker.
source: Glutamate neurons are also prevalent in VTA and overlap with other populations such that ~25% of VTA glutamate neurons co-express a DA marker and ~25% express a GABA marker (Conrad et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2023; Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Approximately 25% of VTA glutamate neurons express a GABA marker.
source: Glutamate neurons are also prevalent in VTA and overlap with other populations such that ~25% of VTA glutamate neurons co-express a DA marker and ~25% express a GABA marker (Conrad et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2023; Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VTA glutamate neurons release glutamate locally within VTA.
source: VTA glutamate neurons release glutamate locally within VTA and from distal axons in medial NAc, PFC, VP, LHb, and elsewhere (Dobi et al., 2010; Gorelova et al., 2012; Hnasko et al., 2012; Root et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2014; Yamaguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VTA glutamate neurons release glutamate from distal axons in medial NAc, PFC, VP, LHb, and elsewhere.
source: VTA glutamate neurons release glutamate locally within VTA and from distal axons in medial NAc, PFC, VP, LHb, and elsewhere (Dobi et al., 2010; Gorelova et al., 2012; Hnasko et al., 2012; Root et al., 2014; Taylor et al., 2014; Yamaguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: DA signals can induce or correlate with distinct behavioral responses depending on their projection targets.
source: It is now understood that DA signals can induce or correlate with distinct behavioral responses depending on their projection targets (Azcorra et al., 2023; Badrinarayan et al., 2012; de Jong et al., 2019; Faget et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activating VTA GABA neurons either locally within VTA or from distal processes can drive behavioral avoidance.
source: For example, activating VTA GABA neurons either locally within VTA or from distal processes can drive behavioral avoidance, disrupt reward seeking, or modify opioid reinforcement (Corre et al., 2018; Root et al., 2020; Shields et al., 2021; Soden et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activating VTA GABA neurons either locally within VTA or from distal processes can disrupt reward seeking.
source: For example, activating VTA GABA neurons either locally within VTA or from distal processes can drive behavioral avoidance, disrupt reward seeking, or modify opioid reinforcement (Corre et al., 2018; Root et al., 2020; Shields et al., 2021; Soden et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activating VTA GABA neurons either locally within VTA or from distal processes can modify opioid reinforcement.
source: For example, activating VTA GABA neurons either locally within VTA or from distal processes can drive behavioral avoidance, disrupt reward seeking, or modify opioid reinforcement (Corre et al., 2018; Root et al., 2020; Shields et al., 2021; Soden et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2012; van Zessen et al., 2012; Zhou et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Stimulation of VTA GABA projections to LHb can be rewarding.
source: On the other hand, stimulation of VTA GABA projections to LHb can be rewarding (Lammel et al., 2015; Stamatakis et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Stimulation of VTA glutamate neurons can drive robust positive reinforcement or behavioral avoidance depending on the projection target and behavioral assay.
source: Likewise, stimulation of VTA glutamate neurons can drive robust positive reinforcement or behavioral avoidance depending on the projection target and behavioral assay (Root et al., 2018; Root et al., 2014; Wang et al., 2015; Yoo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of VTA glutamate projections to NAc drives positive reinforcement through the release of glutamate.
source: For example, activation of VTA glutamate projections to NAc drives positive reinforcement through the release of glutamate and avoidance via DA co-release (Warlow et al., 2024; Zell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Activation of VTA glutamate projections to NAc drives avoidance via DA co-release.
source: For example, activation of VTA glutamate projections to NAc drives positive reinforcement through the release of glutamate and avoidance via DA co-release (Warlow et al., 2024; Zell et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitory inputs to VTA from lateral hypothalamus can drive positive reinforcement and approach behaviors through inhibition of VTA GABA neurons and disinhibition of VTA DA neurons.
source: For example, inhibitory inputs to VTA from lateral hypothalamus, bed nucleus of stria terminalis, or VP can drive positive reinforcement and approach behaviors through inhibition of VTA GABA neurons and disinhibition of VTA DA neurons (Faget et al., 2024; Nieh et al., 2015; Soden et al., 2020; Soden et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitory inputs to VTA from bed nucleus of stria terminalis can drive positive reinforcement and approach behaviors through inhibition of VTA GABA neurons and disinhibition of VTA DA neurons.
source: For example, inhibitory inputs to VTA from lateral hypothalamus, bed nucleus of stria terminalis, or VP can drive positive reinforcement and approach behaviors through inhibition of VTA GABA neurons and disinhibition of VTA DA neurons (Faget et al., 2024; Nieh et al., 2015; Soden et al., 2020; Soden et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibitory inputs to VTA from VP can drive positive reinforcement and approach behaviors through inhibition of VTA GABA neurons and disinhibition of VTA DA neurons.
source: For example, inhibitory inputs to VTA from lateral hypothalamus, bed nucleus of stria terminalis, or VP can drive positive reinforcement and approach behaviors through inhibition of VTA GABA neurons and disinhibition of VTA DA neurons (Faget et al., 2024; Nieh et al., 2015; Soden et al., 2020; Soden et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: VTA GABA circuits appear to be critical for the generation of DA reward prediction error signals.
source: VTA GABA circuits also appear to be critical for the generation of DA reward prediction error signals (Eshel et al., 2015; Keiflin and Janak, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Drugs of abuse can induce rapid or plastic changes in DA signaling through mechanisms that depend on intra-VTA GABA transmission.
source: Moreover, drugs of abuse can induce rapid or plastic changes in DA signaling through mechanisms that depend on intra-VTA GABA transmission (Corre et al., 2018; Gomez et al., 2019; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Ostroumov and Dani, 2018; Ting-A-Kee and van der Kooy, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists directly inhibit non-DA VTA neurons.
source: Indeed, the observation that Mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists directly inhibit non-DA VTA neurons and produce disinhibitory effects on VTA DA neurons (Johnson and North, 1992) helped establish the notion of VTA interneurons into current models of VTA architecture.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists produce disinhibitory effects on VTA DA neurons.
source: Indeed, the observation that Mu-opioid receptor (MOR) agonists directly inhibit non-DA VTA neurons and produce disinhibitory effects on VTA DA neurons (Johnson and North, 1992) helped establish the notion of VTA interneurons into current models of VTA architecture.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: No molecular or physiological feature has been described that can clearly distinguish VTA GABA interneurons from GABA projection neurons.
source: However, no molecular or physiological feature has been described that can clearly distinguish VTA GABA interneurons from GABA projection neurons.
evidence: This is an assertion about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Parvalbumin (PV) is a marker of interneurons in cortex and striatum.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) is a marker of interneurons in cortex and striatum (Kawaguchi, 1993; Kawaguchi and Kondo, 2002; Tepper et al., 2018), but is also expressed in VTA GABA neurons (Olson and Nestler, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Parvalbumin is expressed in VTA GABA neurons.
source: Parvalbumin (PV) is a marker of interneurons in cortex and striatum (Kawaguchi, 1993; Kawaguchi and Kondo, 2002; Tepper et al., 2018), but is also expressed in VTA GABA neurons (Olson and Nestler, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Injections into VTA of PV-Cre mice labeled neurons located in medial VTA.
source: Injections into VTA of PV-Cre mice labeled neurons located in medial VTA.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PV-Cre labeled neurons in VTA project densely to lateral habenula (LHb).
source: We also detected a dense concentration of axonal fibers in LHb, with scant labeling in other known VTA projection targets (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PV labels VTA projection neurons and PV is not a selective marker of VTA interneurons.
source: These data suggest that PV labels VTA projection neurons and PV is not a selective marker of VTA interneurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical tracing data.

claim: Somatostatin (SST) is an interneuron marker in cortex.
source: Like PV, somatostatin (SST) is an interneuron marker in cortex (Kawaguchi and Kondo, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SST is expressed in VTA GABA neurons that can inhibit neighboring VTA DA neurons.
source: SST is expressed in VTA GABA neurons that can inhibit neighboring VTA DA neurons (Nagaeva et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: SST-Cre labeled neurons in VTA project with notably dense labeling in VP.
source: We again identified axons in distal targets, here with notably dense labeling in VP.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: MOR is expressed in VTA GABA neurons.
source: MOR is expressed in VTA GABA neurons, inhibiting GABA release from synapses on to VTA DA neurons, thereby increasing DA neuron firing, and is often described as a marker of VTA interneurons (Gysling and Wang, 1983; Johnson and North, 1992; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Nestler, 2005; Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MOR inhibits GABA release from synapses on to VTA DA neurons, thereby increasing DA neuron firing.
source: MOR is expressed in VTA GABA neurons, inhibiting GABA release from synapses on to VTA DA neurons, thereby increasing DA neuron firing, and is often described as a marker of VTA interneurons (Gysling and Wang, 1983; Johnson and North, 1992; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Nestler, 2005; Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MOR is often described as a marker of VTA interneurons.
source: MOR is expressed in VTA GABA neurons, inhibiting GABA release from synapses on to VTA DA neurons, thereby increasing DA neuron firing, and is often described as a marker of VTA interneurons (Gysling and Wang, 1983; Johnson and North, 1992; Lüscher and Malenka, 2011; Nestler, 2005; Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: MOR-Cre labeled neurons in VTA project to PFC, NAc, LHb, and especially VP.
source: Injections into MOR-Cre mice led to labeled neurons throughout VTA, but also labeled axons in PFC, NAc, LHb, and especially VP (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Neurotensin (NTS) is expressed in a subpopulation of VTA GABA neurons.
source: Neurotensin (NTS) is expressed in a subpopulation of VTA GABA neurons (Phillips et al., 2022) and NTS can stimulate mesolimbic DA cells through activation of NTS receptor 1 (Cáceda et al., 2006; Kalivas et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NTS can stimulate mesolimbic DA cells through activation of NTS receptor 1.
source: Neurotensin (NTS) is expressed in a subpopulation of VTA GABA neurons (Phillips et al., 2022) and NTS can stimulate mesolimbic DA cells through activation of NTS receptor 1 (Cáceda et al., 2006; Kalivas et al., 1983).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: NTS-Cre labeled neurons in VTA project to VP, with weaker labeling in other VTA projection sites.
source: Injections into NTS-Cre mice labeled neurons in VTA, as well as axons in VP, with weaker labeling in other VTA projection sites (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In PV-Cre mice, only 2% of mCherry-labeled VTA neurons expressed TH.
source: In all cases only a minority of mCherry-labeled neurons expressed TH, ranging from 2% for PV to 12% for NTS (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In NTS-Cre mice, 12% of mCherry-labeled VTA neurons expressed TH.
source: In all cases only a minority of mCherry-labeled neurons expressed TH, ranging from 2% for PV to 12% for NTS (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PV, SST, MOR, and NTS markers label primarily non-DA neurons in VTA.
source: In total, our data suggest that these four markers label primarily non-DA neurons in VTA, but that none are selective for interneurons, and instead are inclusive of VTA projection neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the colocalization data.

claim: None of the markers PV, SST, MOR, and NTS are selective for interneurons.
source: In total, our data suggest that these four markers label primarily non-DA neurons in VTA, but that none are selective for interneurons, and instead are inclusive of VTA projection neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical tracing data.

claim: PV, SST, MOR, and NTS markers are inclusive of VTA projection neurons.
source: In total, our data suggest that these four markers label primarily non-DA neurons in VTA, but that none are selective for interneurons, and instead are inclusive of VTA projection neurons.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical tracing data.

claim: LHb-projecting PV-Cre neurons in VTA make local synapses within VTA proximal to TH-positive DA neurons.
source: Using high magnification we observed Syn:Ruby puncta proximal to TH-positive cells in VTA (Figure 2D, J), suggesting that these VTA projection neurons collateralize within VTA and synapse on to DA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: VP-projecting SST-Cre neurons in VTA make local synapses within VTA proximal to TH-positive DA neurons.
source: Using high magnification we observed Syn:Ruby puncta proximal to TH-positive cells in VTA (Figure 2D, J), suggesting that these VTA projection neurons collateralize within VTA and synapse on to DA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: VP-projecting MOR-Cre neurons in VTA make local synapses within VTA proximal to TH-positive DA neurons.
source: Using high magnification, we observed Syn:Ruby puncta proximal to TH-positive VTA neurons, again suggestive of synapses made within VTA by labeled projection neurons (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: VP-projecting NTS-Cre neurons in VTA make local synapses within VTA.
source: Using the same approach to target VP-projecting neurons in NTS-Cre mice we found similar results, with GFP-positive soma in VTA and Syn:Ruby-positive puncta in both VTA (Figure 3I, J) and VP (Figure 3K, L), though signals were notably less dense.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 3I-J.

claim: Multiple markers that had been suggested to label putative interneurons instead label VTA projection neurons that may make local synapses through axon collaterals.
source: These results corroborate the findings in Figure 1 and suggest that multiple markers that had been suggested to label putative interneurons instead label VTA projection neurons that may make local synapses through axon collaterals.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the anatomical data in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: PV, SST, MOR, and NTS neurons in VTA express GABA markers or release GABA.
source: There is evidence indicating that PV, SST, MOR, and NTS neurons in VTA express GABA markers or release GABA (Nagaeva et al., 2020; Olson and Nestler, 2007; Phillips et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Some neurons positive for PV, SST, MOR, and NTS markers may express VGLUT2 and release glutamate.
source: However, some neurons positive for those markers may express VGLUT2 and release glutamate (Miranda-Barrientos et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: NAc-projecting VGAT-Cre neurons in VTA make local collaterals on to VTA DA neurons.
source: At higher magnification, we observed a pattern of GFP fibers and Syn:Ruby puncta surrounding TH-positive cell bodies (Figure 4C, D), suggesting that NAc-projectors make collaterals on to VTA DA neurons.
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 4C-D.

claim: NAc-projecting VGLUT2-Cre neurons in VTA make local collaterals within VTA.
source: We observed similar results when using VGLUT2-Cre mice, suggesting that NAc-projecting VTA glutamate neurons can also make local collaterals within VTA (Figure 4G–L).
evidence: This is supported by anatomical data shown in Figure 4G-L.

claim: VTA glutamate cell bodies are concentrated in medial VTA.
source: As expected VTA glutamate cell bodies were concentrated in medial VTA, where they are most dense (Conrad et al., 2024; Kawano et al., 2006; Yamaguchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and observed in Figure 4H.

claim: 59% of ChR2:mCherry-negative VTA neurons displayed optogenetic-evoked postsynaptic currents when NAc-projecting VTA neurons were stimulated.
source: We patched ChR2:mCherry-negative VTA neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), flashed 2 ms blue light pulses, and observed oPSCs in 59% of neurons; 44% displayed short-latency oIPSCs (mean 84 ± 17 pA), 6% had short-latency oEPSCs (mean –28 ± 6 pA), 41% had no response (responses less than 5 pA were considered unconnected), and 11% had oPSCs with long latency to onset (>5 ms) (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: 44% of ChR2:mCherry-negative VTA neurons displayed short-latency oIPSCs when NAc-projecting VTA neurons were stimulated.
source: We patched ChR2:mCherry-negative VTA neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), flashed 2 ms blue light pulses, and observed oPSCs in 59% of neurons; 44% displayed short-latency oIPSCs (mean 84 ± 17 pA), 6% had short-latency oEPSCs (mean –28 ± 6 pA), 41% had no response (responses less than 5 pA were considered unconnected), and 11% had oPSCs with long latency to onset (>5 ms) (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: 6% of ChR2:mCherry-negative VTA neurons displayed short-latency oEPSCs when NAc-projecting VTA neurons were stimulated.
source: We patched ChR2:mCherry-negative VTA neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), flashed 2 ms blue light pulses, and observed oPSCs in 59% of neurons; 44% displayed short-latency oIPSCs (mean 84 ± 17 pA), 6% had short-latency oEPSCs (mean –28 ± 6 pA), 41% had no response (responses less than 5 pA were considered unconnected), and 11% had oPSCs with long latency to onset (>5 ms) (Figure 5E, F).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5E-F.

claim: The GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX) blocked oIPSCs.
source: The GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX) blocked oIPSCs while oEPSCs were blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist DNQX (Figure 5G, H), confirming that these responses are mediated by evoked GABA or glutamate release, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: The AMPA receptor antagonist DNQX blocked oEPSCs.
source: The GABAA receptor antagonist picrotoxin (PTX) blocked oIPSCs while oEPSCs were blocked by the AMPA receptor antagonist DNQX (Figure 5G, H), confirming that these responses are mediated by evoked GABA or glutamate release, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5G-H.

claim: Most oIPSCs displayed onset latencies more than 2 ms and less than 5 ms, consistent with monosynaptic connectivity.
source: Most responses displayed onset latencies more than 2 ms and less than 5 ms, consistent with monosynaptic connectivity (3.2 ± 0.1 and 3.8 ± 0.2 ms for oIPSCs and oEPSCs, respectively) (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Most oEPSCs displayed onset latencies more than 2 ms and less than 5 ms, consistent with monosynaptic connectivity.
source: Most responses displayed onset latencies more than 2 ms and less than 5 ms, consistent with monosynaptic connectivity (3.2 ± 0.1 and 3.8 ± 0.2 ms for oIPSCs and oEPSCs, respectively) (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The amplitude of oPSCs was diminished following the application of tetrodotoxin (TTX).
source: We found that the amplitude of oPSCs was diminished following the application of the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, voltage-gated sodium channel are necessary for the propagation of action potentials), and that oPSCs recovered with bath application of the inhibitor of voltage-sensitive potassium channels 4-aminopyridine (4AP).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5J-M.

claim: oPSCs recovered with bath application of 4-aminopyridine (4AP).
source: We found that the amplitude of oPSCs was diminished following the application of the voltage-gated sodium channel blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX, voltage-gated sodium channel are necessary for the propagation of action potentials), and that oPSCs recovered with bath application of the inhibitor of voltage-sensitive potassium channels 4-aminopyridine (4AP).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5J-M.

claim: Eight out of nine TTX-diminished oIPSCs were restored by the application of 4AP.
source: When this strategy was applied to oIPSCs (Figure 5J), eight out of nine TTX-diminished currents were restored by the application of 4AP (Figure 5J, K).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5J-K.

claim: Four of seven oEPSCs were recovered by 4AP.
source: Similarly, four of seven oEPSCs were recovered by 4AP (Figure 5L, M).
evidence: This is supported by pharmacological data shown in Figure 5L-M.

claim: 3 of 4 neurons that failed to recover with 4AP had a latency >5 ms.
source: We plotted the latency of oPSC onset against the percent oPSC recovery mediated by 4AP and found that 3 of 4 neurons that failed to recover had a latency >5 ms, whereas only 1 of 13 neurons that had a latency <5 ms failed to recover (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: Only 1 of 13 neurons that had a latency <5 ms failed to recover with 4AP.
source: We plotted the latency of oPSC onset against the percent oPSC recovery mediated by 4AP and found that 3 of 4 neurons that failed to recover had a latency >5 ms, whereas only 1 of 13 neurons that had a latency <5 ms failed to recover (Figure 5N).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5N.

claim: 5 ms was used as a 'short-latency' cutoff to consider an oPSC as monosynaptic.
source: Therefore, we used 5 ms as a 'short-latency' cutoff to consider an oPSC as monosynaptic.
evidence: This is a methodological decision based on the pharmacological data.

claim: The proportion of neurons with oEPSCs versus oIPSCs for long-latency responses (8:2) was strikingly greater than that for short-latency responses (6:41).
